text: Figure 6 : REPL-call composition along trajectories. Calls from all 12 LLMs are combined over normalized trajectory progress [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ; each agent call belongs to exactly one category. State query counts accepted read-only perception calls of Table 1 ( view_board , get_legal_moves , get_history ; only get_history under Restricted observation); other rejected covers unknown or malformed commands, think calls without reasoning, and over-limit or disabled queries. Successful Sighted trials devote more calls to think and fewer to over-budget simulation than failed ones; failed Restricted trials contain a high share of rejected moves throughout. Figure 6 tracks the composition of REPL calls across relative trial progress [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . • Deliberation versus over-budget simulation (Sighted): Successful trials spend 14.9% of their calls on think (17.4% in the first quarter of the trajectory), against 7.6% in failed trials. Failed trials spend 14.2% of calls on simulation requests rejected for exceeding the per-turn budget, against 8.6% in successes; these requests do not advance the board. In the last quarter of failed trajectories, resignation rises to 9.3% of calls. • Persistent illegality (Restricted): In failed Restricted trials, rejected moves make up 33.3% of all calls, against 6.7% in successful ones. The share is high from the start (29.1% in the first quarter, 33.1% in the last), indicating that state-tracking errors arise early rather than accumulating only as the position deteriorates. Across the benchmark, the attacker being checkmated or stalemated remains the dominant failure mode (3,124 Sighted, 2,777 Restricted), while Restricted observation additionally produces 1,178 terminal invalid-action forfeits (Table 11 ). Per-model breakdowns (Figures 14 – 17 ) show the Sighted contrast most clearly for Gemini 3.1 Pro: its wins spend 14.0% of calls on think and 8.7% on over-budget simulation, its losses 2.4% and 19.0%. GPT-5.5 is the exception, interleaving think and simulation up to its final move whether it wins or loses ( think 24.4% versus 21.2%). Under Restricted observation, rejected moves account for 5.2% and 5.6% of calls for Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5 but 77.6% for MiniMax M2.5 and 92.9% for Mistral Large 3. With at most 79 wins per model, these contrasts are descriptive. The Simulation Gap: Checking Legality Is Not Anticipating the Opponent Figure 7 : Simulation checks legality but not the opponent, yet removing it costs wins. (a) Outcomes of all 11,342 Sighted simulation requests; “early stop / capped” comprises 93 legal simulated terminals and four legal prefixes truncated at eight plies. (b) For the 1,677 adopted candidate lines with a legal assumed defender reply, whether the actual defender chose that reply. (c) Controlled ablation on positions each model solved under Sighted observation, three trials per position (Appendix E ): Sighted with and without simulate ; the ablation also disables view_board and get_legal_moves , which neither model uses when the state is refreshed. Bars: pass@1 with 95% case-bootstrap intervals; Δ \Delta : paired difference in points; p p : exact sign test over positions. A natural hypothesis is that a forward simulation sandbox ( 𝒜 sim \mathcal{A}_{\text{sim}} ) lets models verify tactical lines before committing them. The 11,342 simulation requests issued under Sighted observation reveal two limits on what it verifies (Figure 7 a,b); a controlled ablation shows that it nonetheless contributes to conversion (Figure 7 c). Legality falls with line length. Of 6,749 accepted simulation calls, 4,474 executed the complete candidate sequence legally, 2,178 (32.3%) stopped on an illegal move, and the remaining 97 ended early at a simulated terminal or the eight-ply cap. Single-ply requests are almost always legal (96.3% of 2,592 calls), but full-line legality falls to 47.6% for 3–4 plies (1,110/2,332) and 37.4% for 5–8 plies (357/955). Within their own scratchpads, models move pieces through palace boundaries, pins, and missing cannon screens. Assumed opponent replies often differ from the defender’s. Every multi-ply simulated line contains a defender reply chosen by the model itself. Among the 1,677 cases in which an agent adopted the first move of a fully legal line on the real board, the actual defender played a different reply in 49.3% (826/1,677), so the model’s continuation was no longer the line it had checked. These data record disagreement, not the quality of the assumed reply; the sandbox verifies only the model’s own hypothesis about the opponent, which the defender often does not share. The sandbox still helps the strongest models. These limits do not make simulation useless. We re-ran Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5 under Sighted observation with and without simulate , using a shared prompt and a correct check field, on the 20 and 21 positions each had solved at least once in the main evaluation (Appendix E ). The ablation also disables view_board and get_legal_moves , but with the state refreshed after every step both models almost never call them (at most 0.05 calls per turn, against 0.75 and 0.98 simulate calls). Without simulate , pass@1 falls from 48.3% to 33.3% for Gemini and from 39.7% to 25.4% for GPT-5.5 (Figure 7 c). The paired drop is significant for GPT-5.5 ( p = 0.013 p=0.013 ) and has the same sign but is not significant for Gemini ( p = 0.27 p=0.27 ). Simulation thus helps the strongest models find wins even though it verifies only their own hypothesis about the opponent. Without state refreshes, disabling the same commands does not lower pass@1 further (Appendix E ). Figure 8 : Failed trajectories end early; successful ones end at the reference length. Top: plies played divided by the stored mate distance of the case (dashed line: equal length). Boxes summarize failed trials (whiskers: 5th–95th percentiles), points show successful trials, and numbers above the panels give wins out of 357. Triangles mark the 15 wins longer than four times the mate distance, all in JH-084, where the defender loses by perpetual check. Bottom: how failed trials end; lost on board means the attacker was left without a legal move, and action forfeit covers invalid-action, no-command, and action-limit losses. Failing agents are out-raced by the defender. How games end shows the cost of this gap (Figure 8 ). Wins rarely wander: 142 of 178 Sighted wins and 62 of 78 Restricted-observation wins end exactly at the stored mate distance. Failures end early instead: 77.8% of failed Sighted trials and 83.8% of failed Restricted-observation trials stop before that distance. Only 80 of the 8,568 trajectories reach ply 40: 76 end at the turn cap (29 Sighted and 47 Restricted-observation), and four end in a repetition draw on that ply. Most failures are lost on the board, and the share tracks the defender’s counter-threat: 81.8% (Sighted) and 70.4% (Restricted) of failures in the 106 threat-race positions, against 28.2% and 29.8% in the 13 unopposed-mate positions. In the 81 positions whose defender threatens mate in one, 23.8% of Sighted and 30.0% of Restricted-observation trials end at ply 2: the agent’s first move does not stop the threat, and the defender mates at once. Failing agents are thus not stalled but overtaken by replies they did not anticipate. Stronger models survive longer even when they lose: across the 12 models, the median relative length of failed trials rises with the number of wins (Spearman ρ = 0.71 \rho=0.71 Sighted, 0.89 0.89 Restricted observation). Discussion The results suggest two explanations for the gap between finding a good move and converting a won position. Both are interpretations consistent with the data rather than established causes. Amortized policies vs. adversarial search. Converting a won position requires each move to hold up against the defender’s best reply, i.e., an approximation of V ∗ ​ ( s t ) = max a t ⁡ min a def ​ V ∗ ​ ( s t + 1 ) V^{*}(s_{t})=\max_{a_{t}}\min_{a_{\text{def}}}V^{*}(s_{t+1}) over board states s t s_{t} . A language model instead samples each action from an amortized policy P θ ​ ( a t ∣ o t , h t ) P_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t},h_{t}) shaped largely by pre-training. Such a policy can capture familiar motifs, as the 26.1% first-move agreement shows, but nothing in it checks each continuation against counterplay. If a model errs with probability ϵ t \epsilon_{t} at its t t -th move, success on a line of H H moves shrinks roughly as ∏ t = 1 H ( 1 − ϵ t ) \prod_{t=1}^{H}(1-\epsilon_{t}) . This simple picture is consistent with the steep decline in pass@1 with mate distance and with the gap between Gemini’s 45.1% first-move agreement and its 22.1% conversion. It is incomplete: errors are not independent across moves, and wins concentrate on particular positions. Simulation checks legality, not the opponent. The agent writes both sides of every simulated line. A third of accepted simulations stop on an illegal move, and when a legal line began with the move actually played, the real defender chose a different reply in about half of the cases (Section 6 ). This does not show that the imagined replies were bad, since several defenses can be equally strong, but it does show that the sandbox cannot supply the opponent’s choices. Agents that rely on self-authored rollouts in adversarial settings still need an external source of opponent behavior. Implications for agent evaluation. (i) Evaluate closed-loop conversion: agreement on the first move does not imply the ability to finish the game, so benchmarks should include play against an active opponent. (ii) Report reliability alongside coverage: pass@ k k and pass^k diverge sharply here and should be reported together. (iii) Vary one affordance at a time: Restricted observation more than halves pass@1, yet a controlled ablation attributes much of that drop to its prompt and feedback rather than the missing board, so observation settings should differ only in the affordance under test. Conclusion We introduced XiangqiBench , an executable benchmark in which language agents must convert search-supported winning Xiangqi endgames into checkmate against an engine defender. Across 8,568 trajectories from 12 frontier LLMs, finding the move is not winning the game: first-move agreement, pass@3, and self-authored simulation each overstate closed-loop success. Closing these gaps likely takes more than better single-step proposals; agents must win reliably and anticipate how the opponent responds. XiangqiBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring both. References Abdulhai et al. (2025) M. Abdulhai, I. White, C. V. Snell, C. Sun, J. Hong, Y. Zhai, K. Xu, and S.
